## Required Properties

Framework name, framework/adapter packages, explicit case mechanism, fixture
lifecycle, and the filtered test command.

```json

- NUnit is the default framework for .NET automated tests. In an established
  project that deliberately uses another framework, follow that convention. Do
  not introduce a second test framework without a concrete reason.
- Use normal NUnit conventions: `[TestFixture]` classes, `[Test]` for single
  scenarios, `[SetUp]`/`[OneTimeSetUp]` with matching teardown for fixture
  lifetime, and `Assert.That` constraint assertions. The explicit case tables
  required by `testing.md` § Test Readability are written as `[TestCase]` rows
  rather than `TestCaseSource` generators.

- Create test projects with the NUnit template (`dotnet new nunit`) at the
  locations and with the references the `project-structure` workflow defines,
  then remove properties duplicated by `Directory.Build.props` and package
  versions duplicated by Central Package Management.
- Packages (through `add-dependency`): `NUnit`, `NUnit3TestAdapter`,
  `Microsoft.NET.Test.Sdk`; `Microsoft.AspNetCore.Mvc.Testing` for integration
  tests; `Microsoft.Extensions.TimeProvider.Testing` when `FakeTimeProvider` is
  needed.
- Run a subset with `dotnet test --filter "FullyQualifiedName~OrdersApiTests"`.

| Scenario | Default approach |
|---|---|
| Pure business rule | NUnit unit test |
| Application orchestration | Unit test with controlled boundary doubles when useful |
| Full API pipeline | `WebApplicationFactory<Program>` |
| Important persistence/provider behavior | Integration test using the actual provider |
| Simple API integration where provider specifics are irrelevant | Lightweight isolated relational test database may be sufficient |
| Time-dependent behavior | `TimeProvider` / `FakeTimeProvider` |
| External HTTP dependency | Stub handler or local fake server |
| Reproduced bug | Focused regression test |
| Temporary behavioral check | Convert to maintained coverage or confirm equivalent existing coverage |
| Deployment/basic health | Smoke test |

- Backend test stack (Decided): NUnit with its test adapter for .NET automated
  tests; `Microsoft.AspNetCore.Mvc.Testing` with `WebApplicationFactory<Program>`
  is the baseline for ASP.NET Core integration tests; Testcontainers is
  conditional and is added only when isolated real-provider tests justify it.
- Backend test projects are placed by the architecture frame

| backend-testing | leaf, required | selected | nunit | — |

canonical_policy.name: Choose narrowest useful test level
canonical_policy.normalized_policy: Choose the narrowest test level that meaningfully verifies the behavior; use integration tests when framework/persistence/HTTP wiring is the subject; no fixed unit/integration ratio is required.

reviews.boundary_analysis: Narrowest meaningful level/no fixed ratio matches; no requirement to duplicate naturally covered behavior. Small/full versus large/risk-scoped suiteEXTRA0245, version-differenceEXTRA0098 and test-doubleBF0037 already prior.

context_quotes:
Choose the narrowest test level that meaningfully verifies the behavior. Use
unit tests for isolated business, domain, or application logic; use integration
tests when framework wiring, HTTP, persistence, serialization, authentication,
or component interaction is what matters. No fixed unit/integration ratio is
required, and neither level is required for behavior naturally verified by the
other.

For small finite input or state spaces, prefer explicit declarative test cases
over loops, branches, LINQ, or generated case machinery inside tests; state
expected results rather than computing them. Prefer one observable scenario per
test; a multi-step test is appropriate when the sequence itself is the behavior.

## Test Doubles

Use fakes, stubs, or mocks when they make an isolated test clearer; do not mock
every dependency mechanically, and do not forbid mocking project-owned
abstractions. When important behavior depends on real persistence, provider, or
HTTP semantics, prefer an integration test over reproducing that behavior with
mocks.

When the project has chosen Angular Material, use its components consistently
for common UI primitives where they satisfy the requirement. Do not add it
automatically to a project that has not chosen it, and do not wrap every
Material component in a custom abstraction without a concrete reason.

## API Client Generation

When OpenAPI client generation is adopted, treat generated code as generated:
keep it separate from handwritten feature logic and regenerate it when the API
contract changes (`build-fix` § Generated Code). Backend contract
documentation: `swagger` skill.

## Testing

Useful frontend test targets: meaningful component behavior, validation,
data-access request mapping, important route/auth behavior, and complex
reactive state. Do not test Angular framework internals. End-to-end tests focus
on a small number of important user workflows unless the project requires
broader E2E coverage; do not duplicate the same behavior at every test level.

When versions coexist, test meaningful differences: version routing,
version-specific response shape, a deprecated version still operational during
its support period, unsupported-version behavior, and shared Application
behavior staying consistent where intended. Do not duplicate identical tests
merely because two versions share Application behavior.

Replace repository and external-service abstractions with controlled test
doubles and focus assertions on the use-case result and meaningful side
effects. A verification such as "repository method X was called once" is
useful only when that interaction is part of the contract. When important
behavior depends on persistence semantics, transactions, DI wiring,
serialization, or HTTP, prefer an integration test.

| Scenario | Default approach |
|---|---|
| Pure business rule | NUnit unit test |
| Application orchestration | Unit test with controlled boundary doubles when useful |
| Full API pipeline | `WebApplicationFactory<Program>` |
| Important persistence/provider behavior | Integration test using the actual provider |
| Simple API integration where provider specifics are irrelevant | Lightweight isolated relational test database may be sufficient |
| Time-dependent behavior | `TimeProvider` / `FakeTimeProvider` |
| External HTTP dependency | Stub handler or local fake server |
| Reproduced bug | Focused regression test |
| Temporary behavioral check | Convert to maintained coverage or confirm equivalent existing coverage |
| Deployment/basic health | Smoke test |

Run the tests covering the changed area (for example `dotnet test --no-build`,
and the frontend test script when `package.json` defines one — inspect
`package.json` rather than assuming a runner). For small solutions run the
complete suite; for large ones run affected test projects first, then any
broader suite the change risk requires. Investigate every newly failing
relevant test; do not dismiss a failure as unrelated without checking it.

Test authorization behavior for important protected operations: an
unauthenticated request → `401`; an authenticated caller without permission →
`403`; a permitted caller → expected success; resource-specific ownership rules;
anonymous endpoints remain accessible when intended. Verify observable behavior
rather than the mere presence of `[Authorize]`.

Test cache behavior when it affects observable correctness: stale entries are
invalidated after a successful mutation, tenant/user keys are isolated, a miss
falls back correctly, an outage follows the intended failure policy. Do not
unit-test framework cache internals.

a regression test when recurrence is plausible. Check that behavioral probes
were preserved (`verify` § Preserve Behavioral Verification). Do not request
duplicate tests when equivalent coverage exists.

behavior under test clearer.

matters; an isolated real-provider setup such as Testcontainers is optional,
not mandatory for every project or integration test. Do not claim provider
fidelity from a different or non-relational provider; the provider binding is
in `.claude/rules/persistence-technology.md`.

Provider fidelity matters for provider-specific SQL, constraints, transactions,
locking/concurrency, indexes, raw SQL, provider-specific mappings, and
migrations — use the actual provider (`.claude/rules/persistence-technology.md`

real database. When provider fidelity does not matter, a lighter isolated
relational database may be acceptable for application/API integration tests;
state the trade-off. For a true unit test, a fake repository is often clearer
than any database.
